Here's the ladder for stays under twenty eight nights, as of now.
Flexible gives a full refund until twenty four hours before check in.
Moderate, until five days before.
Limited, which is new for bookings from October first, twenty twenty five, gives a full refund until fourteen days out, and half back between seven and fourteen days.
Firm gives a full refund until thirty days out, and half back between seven and thirty days.
And inside seven days on Limited or Firm?
The host is paid in full.
Strict and the super strict policies exist too, but they're invitation only.
And every standard policy has a twenty four hour free cancellation window, as long as the booking was made at least seven days before check in.

So how does a host actually choose?
Start with how far ahead your guests book.
If most of your bookings come in two or three weeks out, a thirty day Firm policy means almost every guest books inside the strict part.

If your summer weekends book in February, Firm protects dates you genuinely can't refill.
So the policy should match your booking window.
That's the rule of thumb I'd use.

How many days between booking and check in?
If it's usually under two weeks, Flexible or Moderate costs you very little.
If it's months, Limited or Firm starts to earn its keep.

events.text: Now the trap.
Vrbo has a policy called Firm too, right?
It does, and it means something very different.
On Airbnb, Firm gives a full refund until thirty days out.
On Vrbo, Firm gives a full refund only until sixty days out, and half back between thirty and sixty days.
So a host who picks Firm on both thinks they have one policy.
And they actually have two.
A guest who cancels forty five days out gets everything back on one platform and half on the other.
Vrbo has seven options in all.
Day before, Lenient, Relaxed, Moderate, Firm, Strict and No refund.
